claims.claim: Hydroponic / indoor-grown lettuce is priced at a premium over conventionally grown product at retail.
claims.episode_span: one university cost study found vertical-farm lettuce in New York and Chicago cost roughly twice as much to produce as California field lettuce shipped in
claims.source_title: Behind the greens: Why hydroponic lettuce is not competitive yet - AgFunderNews
claims.supporting_quote: Hydroponic and locally grown product is priced at a premium, even versus organic.

claims.claim: Current specific energy consumption for lettuce in indoor vertical farms is about 10-18 kWh per kilogram (total).
claims.episode_span: Total electricity use commonly runs 10–18 kWh per kilogram of fresh produce in reported installations, with lighting the largest share and cooling and dehumidification most of the remainder.
claims.source_title: Solve Vertical Farming Energy Problem: 5 Real Solutions (verticalfarming.blog)
claims.supporting_quote: current specific energy consumption for lettuce production in indoor vertical farms at 10–18 kWh per kilogram

claims.claim: Field-grown lettuce uses roughly 1-5 kWh/kg of (almost entirely indirect) energy, far below vertical-farm figures.
claims.episode_span: Field agriculture, by contrast, receives its photons at zero direct cost and sheds heat to the open air, so its cost structure never encounters this double burden.
claims.source_title: Solve Vertical Farming Energy Problem: 5 Real Solutions (verticalfarming.blog)
claims.supporting_quote: In a traditional open field, the equivalent figure is 1–5 kWh/kg – almost entirely indirect energy (machinery, fertilizer, irrigation).

claims.claim: Lettuce is about 94.9 percent water, so nearly all of a head's mass is water rather than dry matter.
claims.episode_span: A typical head of lettuce contains on the order of a few tens of grams of dry matter, mostly carbohydrates and water, whose commodity value as bulk biomass is measured in cents.
claims.supporting_quote: The high water content of lettuce (94.9 percent) creates problems when attempting to preserve the plant

claims.claim: A theoretical future benchmark of 3.1-7.4 kWh/kg has been identified for vertical-farm lettuce, well below current reported energy use.
claims.episode_span: combined with published energy-use figures per kilogram that fall well below the current reported range.
claims.source_title: Solve Vertical Farming Energy Problem: 5 Real Solutions (verticalfarming.blog)
claims.supporting_quote: The same study identifies a theoretical future benchmark of 3.1–7.4 kWh/kg as the direction technology is moving

claims.claim: Producing one kilogram of lettuce in a vertical farm takes around 12.5 kWh of electricity (roughly 10-20 kWh depending on the setup).
claims.episode_span: Total electricity use commonly runs 10–18 kWh per kilogram of fresh produce in reported installations
claims.source_title: Vertical farming: a local solution for greens, but not feeding the world any time soon — Hannah Ritchie (Sustainability by numbers)
claims.supporting_quote: It’s estimated that it takes around 12.5 kWh to produce one kilogram of lettuce.

claims.claim: Typically 60-80% of a vertical farm's electricity goes to lighting, with most of the remainder to heating or cooling.
claims.episode_span: with lighting the largest share and cooling and dehumidification most of the remainder
claims.source_title: Vertical farming: a local solution for greens, but not feeding the world any time soon — Hannah Ritchie (Sustainability by numbers)
claims.supporting_quote: Most of it — typically 60% to 80% — is for lighting, which essentially mimics the sun to produce the light needed for photosynthesis. The rest is used for heating or cooling

claims.claim: Cereals are not going to be produced in vertical farms any time soon; one published estimate puts lighting cost alone at about 100 times the market price of wheat or rice.
claims.episode_span: calories and staple grains will remain uneconomic indoors at present electricity prices
claims.source_title: Vertical farming: a local solution for greens, but not feeding the world any time soon — Hannah Ritchie (Sustainability by numbers)
claims.supporting_quote: Another paper — published in Nature — estimated that lighting alone costs around 100 times the market price of wheat or rice.

claims.claim: Cornell's Neil Mattson holds that vertical farms will be cost-effective only when renewable-energy prices fall; operators are already experimenting with solar and wind to cut energy bills.
claims.episode_span: One path is to locate facilities where electricity is already near its marginal cost floor, such as regions with persistent surplus renewable generation
claims.source_title: Radically rethinking how we make food | Cornell Controlled Environment Agriculture
claims.supporting_quote: Vertical-farm companies are experimenting with using solar and wind power to reduce their energy bills, but Mattson believes vertical farms will be cost-effective only when renewable-energy prices fall.

claims.claim: Photosynthesis sets a physical floor on biomass per kilowatt-hour: most crops convert just 1-6% of incident light energy into biomass, with a theoretical maximum near 11%.
claims.episode_span: No amount of redesign removes the second law losses when electricity is turned into light and then back into heat
claims.source_title: Vertical farming: a local solution for greens, but not feeding the world any time soon — Hannah Ritchie (Sustainability by numbers)
claims.supporting_quote: Most crops convert just 1% to 6% of solar energy into biomass. The theoretical maximum is around 11%.
